newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin gets surgery go-ahead, doctors optimistic.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin gets surgery go-ahead, doctors optimistic.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin was given the go-ahead for heart surgery on Wednesday and doctors said they were supremely confident the operation would be successful after another six to eight weeks of preparation.
Leading cardiologist Renat Akchurin, expected to head the team that will carry out the operation, told a news conference that the delay was needed to minimise the risk.
"If we operate now, I would say the chance is about 80 percent, but we hope that in six weeks the percentage would be close to 100," he told a news conference.

Other specialists, including pioneering U.S. heart surgeon Michael DeBakey, shared this optimism. "After reviewing all facts I am very encouraged to tell you that the operation is needed, that it should provide excellent results," he said.
"There is no reason why the president should not be restored to full normal activity."
The doctors were speaking after meeting Yeltsin for about two hours at Moscow's Central Clinical Hospital, where the 65-year-old leader has been under close medical observation since September 13.

The doctors set no firm date for the planned bypass operation, which is a relatively routine procedure, barring complications, involving grafting in veins from the leg to relieve Yeltsin's clogged heart arteries.
The president's prolonged stay in hospital and his absence from public life have fuelled speculation about potentially destabilising power struggles brewing behind the scenes.
Kremlin officials have condemned the rumour-mongering as indecent and say the president is in full control of affairs of state, working on documents for up to 2-1/2 hours a day.

The undercurrent of instability in Russia was underlined on Wednesday by security chief Alexander Lebed, who told a Moscow newspaper that the government's failure to pay soldiers' wages could soon spark military uprisings.
"An armed mutiny may take place this autumn," the outspoken ex-paratroop general told the Vechernyaya Moskva daily.

Yeltsin had two heart attacks last year and his current health problems have given his political opponents fresh impetus. Communist leaders have called for him to step down if he is unable to bear the workload required of his office.
Mikhail Gorbachev, the last president of the Soviet Union, added his voice to the communist chorus on Wednesday, urging his former rival to resign.
But the upbeat medical assessment appeared to back up the view of Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, Yeltsin's constitutional substitute, that it is premature to talk of the president standing down.

Chief Kremlin doctor Sergei Mironov said: "The main news today is that the operation will take place. It is necessary." "We were glad to see that DeBakey's position and that of the Russian doctors who treated the president lately coincided."
Andrei Vorobyov, head of the doctors' council which examined Yeltsin, said Yeltsin's vigorous re-election campaign had made things more complicated and led to the six- toeight-week delay.
"The president is likely to spend this time in hospital. He will work, but those are the conditions of preparation for an operation," he said.
Akchurin said: "The president of course is working now but his activity is limited by the preparation for the operation."
Russian financial markets reacted positively to the news, with prices of MinFin bonds rising. Earlier share markets rose following a statement that the operation would go ahead.

The risk of dying in a heart bypass operation is about five percent in Russia, but doctors say it could be greater for Yeltsin if he has serious liver or kidney problems which have not been disclosed.
DeBakey, 88, said said Yeltsin's liver and kidneys were normal. He said he would be permanently available to return to Moscow to advise his Russian colleagues.
Bill Clinton had asked him to make it his "number one priority" and DeBakey said he had accepted the U.S. president's request.
